source_reviews.independent_solution: A light ray is an idealized directed geometrical line representing the local direction and path of light propagation. It is a model of propagation, not a material thread or the whole finite-width beam. In a homogeneous transparent medium under the geometrical-optics approximation it is straight; reflection or refraction can change its direction, so straight everywhere is not an unconditional definition.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Luminous flux Phi_v is optical radiant power evaluated with the visual-response weighting used in photometry: it expresses the light's capacity to produce a visual effect, rather than unweighted radiant energy per second. Its unit is the lumen. Equal radiant powers with different spectral distributions need not have equal luminous fluxes. This is not illuminance (flux per receiving area), luminous intensity (flux per solid angle in a direction), a photon count, or the particular observer's subjective brightness.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Luminous intensity I_v in a specified direction is luminous flux per unit solid angle about that direction. Precisely I_v=dPhi_v/dOmega; its unit is candela, equivalent to lumen per steradian. Phi_v/Omega over a finite angular region is its average intensity unless intensity is uniform over that region. A point-source model neglects source size; it does not force equal intensity in every direction. Total Phi_v=4 pi I applies when the same I holds over all directions, as explicitly stated in the spherical illustration, not to an arbitrary directional point source.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For direct unobstructed illumination of a local receiving surface point in the geometrical point-source model, E=I_v(direction toward that point) cos(alpha)/R^2. Thus it depends on the source's luminous intensity in the relevant direction, distance R from the source to that receiving point, and incidence angle alpha measured to the surface normal, not to the plane. With the other factors fixed it is proportional to I_v and cos(alpha), and inversely proportional to R squared. The illuminated face has a nonnegative incidence cosine: normal incidence gives the maximum for fixed I_v,R and grazing incidence gives zero direct projected contribution. A finite-area Phi/S is average illuminance; it equals each point's illuminance only for a uniform field.

mathematics.independent_solution: Within the stated angular region, DeltaPhi is approximately I times DeltaOmega, hence I approximately equals DeltaPhi/DeltaOmega. This selects A. Area normalization and total flux are different quantities; a total divided by 4 pi gives the angular average, not each directional value for an arbitrary point source.

Phi_total/(4 pi) is the full-sphere angular average. A pointlike source can emit unequal intensities into different directions, so it cannot universally equal each directional intensity.

mathematics.independent_solution: Use the frozen local direct-light relation E=I_v(direction)cos(alpha)/R^2 on these new variants. I doubled gives 2E; R doubled at fixed direction/incidence gives E/4; cos(60 degrees)/cos(0 degrees)=1/2; cos(90 degrees)=0. Point source alone does not enforce isotropy, and rotation changes the cosine. Thus A,B,C,E are the complete true set in both languages.

option_checks.evidence: At fixed R and alpha, E(2I)=2I cos(alpha)/R^2=2E. The option specifies intensity toward the element.
At fixed I in the same emission direction and fixed alpha, E(2R)=I cos(alpha)/(2R)^2=E/4.
Fixed position keeps R and source emission direction unchanged. Turning the local element from normal incidence to 60 degrees changes the cosine from 1 to 1/2.
Negligible source size does not require equal intensity in all directions; directional emission is a counterexample.
At the grazing limit the local plane element's projected area factor is cos(90 degrees)=0, so its direct illuminance is zero under this model.

At one receiving position with positive incident intensity, rotation from normal to 60 degrees halves E although R stays fixed. Even orientations inside the stated range refute any-orientation invariance.
